analysis.one_liner: Raises federal oil and gas royalty rates, ends noncompetitive leases, and adds fracking water-safety rules on public lands.
analysis.headline: The House Natural Resources Committee reported the bill 24-15 in December 2022, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how the government leases public land for oil and gas drilling. It would raise the royalty companies pay on what they pump from 12.5% to at least 18.75%, raise minimum bids and yearly rents, end the practice of handing out leases without competitive bidding, shorten lease terms from 10 years to 5, and publish the names of who bids on and holds leases. It would also protect people who own the surface above federal minerals, and require oil companies to replace water supplies their drilling contaminates, plus order new federal rules for fracking, including water testing before drilling and public disclosure of fracking chemicals [S2, S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would collect more from oil and gas taken from land they own; ranchers and other private landowners sitting above federally owned minerals, who would gain a required agreement with drillers covering damage and reclamation; and residents near fracking operations, who would get water testing and chemical disclosure [S2, S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, ranchers, and people near fracking sites

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum royalty on federal oil and gas leases from the long-standing 12.5% to at least 18.75% of production value, so taxpayers collect more on resources they own
Eliminates noncompetitive leasing, under which tracts could be handed out without any bidding, and moves all leasing to competitive sealed bids with a higher $10-per-acre minimum bid

Requires drillers to replace water supplies contaminated, diminished, or interrupted by drilling, fracking, or production, and directs BLM to issue fracking rules requiring baseline water testing and public disclosure of every chemical used

Requires operators to sign a surface-use agreement with private landowners covering reasonable site use, reclamation, and compensation for damages to crops, forage, and livestock before drilling can begin
Requires public websites listing the identity of every bidder, current and former lessee, and operator, plus notice of every lease transfer and suspension

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies operating on federal land, which would pay higher royalties, rents, minimum bids, and a fee for nominating land for leasing, and would lose the option of noncompetitive leases and 10-year terms

drawbacks.text: Higher royalty, rental, and minimum-bid costs fall on operators leasing federal land, which an honest supporter would acknowledge may make some federal leases less attractive compared with private or state land
The bill cuts lease sales to no more than three per state per year and shortens lease terms from 10 years to 5, which slows the leasing cycle and gives companies shorter windows to develop a lease
New pre-drilling requirements, including water management plans and surface-use agreements, add steps and time before drilling can begin on any given parcel

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: ordinary taxpayers and landowners get more money and more protection; drillers pay more and face more process. The main costs are slower leasing and higher operating costs, which supporters judged worth paying to end below-market royalties, no-bid leases, and unmonitored fracking on public land.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved the bill in May 2021 and formally reported it on December 14, 2022 — the final weeks of the Congress — but House leadership never scheduled a floor vote before the session ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 2, 2021 by Rep. Mike Levin with ten original cosponsors and referred to the Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees
On May 5, 2021, the Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported by a vote of 24 to 15
The committee held the bill for 19 months before formally reporting it, amended, on December 14, 2022 as H. Rept. 117-628, with seven additional Democratic cosponsors added that same month
On December 14, 2022 the Agriculture Committee was discharged and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, but no House floor vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies operating on federal land are better off, because the old terms they lease under — a 12.5% royalty, no-bid leases, and no federal fracking rule — remained in effect.

for.name: Rep. Mike Levin
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 2, 2021 and advanced it through the committee process

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, brought it through his committee's markup, where it was ordered reported 24-15, and formally reported it on December 14, 2022

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Speaker and Majority Leader's office, which controlled the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor after it was placed on the Union Calendar on December 14, 2022; the session ended January 3, 2023 with no vote

against.name: 15 members of the House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported at the May 5, 2021 markup

against.name: House Republican majority of the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took control of the House floor calendar when the new Congress began, ending any realistic prospect of reviving the bill in that form

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were House Democrats; the committee reported it 24-15, though the record does not break the no votes down by party.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal lands
industries.note: The bill would raise their royalty from 12.5% to at least 18.75%, raise minimum bids and annual rents, end noncompetitive leases and 10-year lease terms, and add fracking water rules. The industry currently leases public resources on terms well below what private landowners would charge, so its gain under the status quo is the public's lost revenue.

industries.industry: Companies that nominate public land for leasing
industries.note: The bill creates a fee of at least $15 per acre for submitting an expression of interest in leasing, a cost that did not exist before.
